highlights: The Military Governor proposed establishing a representative Korean interim legislative body to enact ordinances and screen governmental appointments.
Ordinance No. 97 established the Department of Labor, officially recognizing the right of Korean workers to organize unions and engage in collective bargaining.
Cheju-do and the Chuja Archipelago were separated from Cholla-namdo and established as an independent province under Ordinance No. 94.
A nationwide cholera epidemic reached 7,642 reported cases and 4,878 deaths by 31 July, prompting strict travel quarantines and mass vaccinations.
Price ceilings were instituted on 15 July for essential consumer goods, including cotton cloth, rubber shoes, soap, matches, and electric light bulbs.
Type A occupational currency was demonetized and required to be deposited into financial institutions between 1 and 10 July.
The National Police Academy graduated its first class of 55 policewomen on 12 July and its first commissioned officer class on 19 July.

summary: Number 10 of the USAMGIK Summation covers July 1946, documenting a critical juncture in the American occupation of South Korea characterized by administrative institutionalization amid acute socioeconomic distress. Key political and administrative developments include the proposal by the Military Governor for an interim Korean legislative body, the separation of Cheju Island into an independent province, and the promulgation of Ordinances 97 and 98, which established the Department of Labor—recognizing collective bargaining rights—and reorganized the Department of Commerce into separate foreign and domestic commerce bureaus. The occupation faced compounding crises: late June floods severely crippled the national railway network and coal transport, while a virulent cholera epidemic claimed over 4,800 lives, prompting travel bans and the suspension of mail exchanges with Soviet-occupied North Korea. Acute food shortages in Seoul and Inchon forced increased reliance on imported American grain as domestic summer grain collections fell far behind targets. To combat spiraling inflation, USAMGIK imposed price ceilings on staple consumer goods and demonetized Type A military currency. For historians, this report provides invaluable quantitative data on commodity price inflation, police professionalization, prison industries, and massive cross-border repatriation movements.
